blocks.title: Write down the one assumption that could kill you
blocks.text: In 2010 Adani himself named fuel as the one thing that could go wrong, after he had already signed fixed prices. Before you sign a long contract, ask what happens if your biggest cost doubles. If the answer is “we die”, change the contract or change the plan.

chapters.title: The Report, the Indictment, the Comeback

blocks.text: A short seller is an investor who profits when a share price falls. On ==24 January 2023==, a US short seller called Hindenburg Research published its report on the Adani Group, then valued at about $218 billion. It said its two-year investigation showed stock manipulation and accounting fraud, and that it held short positions itself. The group called the report baseless, and a later 413-page response called it a calculated attack on India.

The timing could not have been worse. Adani Enterprises was about to launch an FPO, a follow-on public offer in which a listed company sells new shares, for ==₹20,000 crore==, or $2.45 billion, the biggest of its kind in India. Within two days of trading, seven group companies lost $48 billion. On the first day, the offer got just 1% of the bids it needed. Abu Dhabi's International Holding Company stepped in with $400 million, and the sale scraped through on 31 January.

The next day the shares crashed anyway. Adani Enterprises fell 28% and Credit Suisse stopped accepting group bonds as loan security. Late that night, the company did something unusual. It cancelled a fully subscribed share sale, and gave the money back.
For me, the interest of my investors is paramount and everything is secondary.
blocks.who: Gautam Adani, video message, 2 February 2023

blocks.text: By early February the group's market value had dropped by more than half at its worst, hitting a record low of about ==$82 billion== combined. Adani fell from the third-richest person in the world to outside the top 25 on Forbes' list. Reuters later put the sell-off at $150 billion, The Times of India at $140 billion. Hindenburg's claims were never tested in a trial, and the group denied them all.
Third richest to outside the top 25. Debt makes things fast.
How he survived it

His first problem was a kind of loan called a margin loan. The family had pledged shares as security for borrowings, and when prices fall, lenders demand more security or sell the shares. So the first move was to pay them back early. By 12 March 2023 the family had prepaid ==$2.15 billion== of share-backed loans, plus $500 million on the Ambuja purchase, and pledged holdings fell sharply.

His second move was to stop buying. DB Power, PTC India, SKS Power and Macquarie's roads all went, and a ₹34,900 crore plastics plant was paused. His third was to find a single loud believer. In March 2023, Rajiv Jain of US fund GQG Partners bought shares in four Adani firms for ==₹15,446 crore==, about $1.9 billion. Eleven weeks later that stake was worth ₹23,049 crore. GQG kept buying.
One outside investor can change a story. Know who would call you back.

Then the courts. A six-member Supreme Court committee reported in May 2023 that it could not conclude there was a regulatory failure on price manipulation, though Financial Express noted this was not a clean chit. On 3 January 2024 the Supreme Court refused to order a special investigation and left the matter with SEBI, India's market regulator. Then, a year after the crash, the group's market value had risen 112% from the low. __A crisis met with cash and speed can leave you stronger on paper, though the questions do not go away.__

SEBI's answers came slowly. On 18 September 2025 it closed two matters without penalty, covering alleged transactions with related companies. A day later Reuters reported more than a dozen cases were still open. On 28 September 2026 SEBI ruled it could not prove that Gautam's brother Vinod Adani controlled two offshore funds that held group shares, and dropped that case. It fined two other people ₹20 lakh each for not giving correct information, saying one had made a deliberate attempt to mislead. Separately, Gautam Adani, four group companies and 13 others paid ₹1.48 crore to settle the same shareholding rules case, without admitting or denying anything.
Having considered the matter holistically, I find that the allegations made against noticees are not established,
blocks.who: Kamlesh Chandra Varshney, SEBI whole-time member, 18 September 2025

blocks.text: By then Hindenburg itself had gone. Its founder Nathan Anderson announced in January 2025 that he was disbanding the firm. He wrote that “We shook some empires that we felt needed shaking”. Closing did not prove the report right or wrong, in either direction.
The Brooklyn indictment

Then came a harder blow. On ==20 November 2024== US prosecutors in Brooklyn unsealed an indictment charging Gautam Adani, his nephew Sagar and former Adani Green chief executive Vneet Jaain with securities and wire fraud. They said a wider group had agreed to pay about $265 million in bribes to Indian officials to win solar power contracts, and had then misled US investors about it. The SEC filed a civil case too. These were allegations, which Adani denied, and he was not charged under the US bribery statute itself.

The damage was immediate and practical. Kenya's president cancelled over $2.5 billion in deals the very next day. TotalEnergies, a 20% owner of Adani Green, said it had not been told of the investigation and paused new money. Adani Ports dropped its $553 million request to a US agency for Colombo, and Adani Green pulled out of its Sri Lanka wind projects. By December he had agreed to sell out of Fortune oil for $2 billion.
Until such time when the accusations against the Adani group individuals and their consequences have been clarified, TotalEnergies will not make any new financial contribution
blocks.who: TotalEnergies statement, 25 November 2024

blocks.text: A separate problem surfaced too. In May 2026 Adani Enterprises agreed to pay ==$275 million== to the US Treasury's sanctions office, OFAC. OFAC said the company had bought liquefied petroleum gas from a Dubai trader between November 2023 and June 2025, that the gas came from Iran, and that “Red flags should have put AEL on notice”. The first cargo, worth $5.67 million, came on a 25-year-old tanker, with papers naming Oman as its origin. OFAC called the apparent violations egregious. The company settled without admitting them, and told exchanges the LPG trade was under 1.5% of its revenue.

In 2026 the American case turned. By May, Adani had settled the SEC case, without admitting wrongdoing, for $6 million, with $12 million from Sagar. The Justice Department, now under the Trump administration, asked to drop the charges with prejudice, which means they cannot be brought again.

Why the change? CBS News, citing sources, reported that his lawyer raised a $10 billion US investment in a meeting with officials. The judge ordered Adani to swear an affidavit on it. He said there was no deal, while accepting that his lawyers had proposed the investment as part of a possible resolution. The US Attorney in Brooklyn had rejected that idea in writing.

On ==10 August 2026== Judge Nicholas Garaufis dismissed the fraud charges against Gautam Adani, Sagar Adani and Jaain. He accepted just one of the government's reasons: that the anti-bribery language in Adani Green's documents was generic enough to be mere puffery, the kind of vague claim no investor could rely on. He also made clear this was no endorsement of the department's decision and no opinion on whether the allegations were true. He called the way the decision was reached “highly unusual”.

So how should you read this? No jury ever heard the evidence, and no court decided whether bribes were paid. Adani is free of the charges and did not admit guilt. On 3 September 2026 the same judge refused to drop the case against the five other accused, because the government had not given enough evidence for its reasons. The Justice Department went to an appeals court on 28 September, and the judge filed a brief opposing it in late October, so that fight was still running in early November.
Dismissed is not the same as disproved. Nor is it proof of guilt.

blocks.title: In a crisis, act on cash first and story second
blocks.text: Within seven weeks of the report, Adani repaid the loans that could have forced his shares onto the market, returned ₹20,000 crore, and cancelled deal after deal. Whatever you think of the allegations, that order is worth copying. Fix what can kill you this month before you argue about reputation.

blocks.title: Do not treat a compliance rule as paperwork
blocks.text: A 25-year-old tanker, a Dubai trader and a $5.67 million first shipment became a $275 million settlement. OFAC's point was that the paperwork looked clean, but the red flags were visible. Assign someone to look for what the documents do not say.

Ask how rich Gautam Adani is and you can get four very different answers in the same week. Forbes's real-time page for him showed ==$79.2 billion== on 2 November 2026, ranked 26th in the world. Its India's Richest list, published on 30 September and using 11 September prices, gave “Gautam Adani & family” ==$112.7 billion==, and put him back at number one in India after three years. Bloomberg's index, updated on 1 November, had him at ==$109 billion==, ranked 18th. Hurun's Indian list in September said about $96 billion.

Why the gap? Most of this wealth is not money in a bank. It is a share of companies, multiplied by a share price that changes every second, minus debt that outsiders cannot fully see. Lists also differ on who counts: Forbes's India list explicitly covers a fortune he shares with his family. __Remember this whenever you read a billionaire's net worth: it is an opinion about share prices, not a bank balance.__

blocks.text: Below those sit $12.8 billion in Adani Energy Solutions, $2.32 billion in Adani Total Gas, and $1.75 billion in Ambuja Cements, plus private holdings such as Adani Properties at $4.69 billion, all on Bloomberg's estimate. All the pieces add up to about $120.7 billion. Bloomberg then takes off $11.75 billion of liabilities to reach its $109 billion, and it leaves out the offshore family companies, for lack of public disclosure. In the flagship, the family held 71.97% in September 2026, with 47.43% held by Gautam and his brother Rajesh on behalf of the S.B. Adani Family Trust.
The power company that nearly died is now his second-biggest stake.
How the fortune actually grew

For most of his career he was rich, not record-breaking. The leap came in a few strange years. His fortune was $32.4 billion in December 2020, up $21.1 billion that year. From January 2020 to June 2021, group shares rose between 122% and 819%, while the Sensex rose 27%. By June 2021, Business Today put his wealth at $77 billion, and it asked directly why the shares had risen so much.

For example: in June 2021 Adani Total Gas was valued at ₹1.48 lakh crore on ₹471 crore of profit. Gujarat Gas, a much larger rival, was worth ₹36,921 crore on ₹1,275 crore of profit. One analyst in 2020 called it “FOMO syndrome”, the fear of missing out. Business Today said the family then owned 56% to 75% of the listed firms, so ratings like that made it far richer on paper.

He peaked at about ==$150 billion== in 2022, briefly one of the richest people on the planet. After the Hindenburg report it fell far faster than it rose. That swing shows the risk in the structure. Forbes describes his growth as debt-financed acquisitions and close ties to Prime Minister Modi. He has said he got no special favours and keeps good relations across parties, and The Times of India notes the group invests in states run by different parties. Read those claims side by side and judge for yourself.
The market is having FOMO syndrome when it comes to Adani stocks,
blocks.who: Sanjiv Bhasin, IIFL Securities, to Bloomberg, December 2020

blocks.text: The machine underneath

Strip away the share prices and there is still a very large machine. In FY26, the group reported EBITDA of ==₹94,834 crore==. EBITDA means operating earnings before interest, tax and wear on assets, a rough measure of cash generated. It spent ₹1,52,967 crore on new projects in one year, which it says is the highest ever by any Indian company and about equal to what it built in its first 25 years.

It reports net debt of 3.3 times EBITDA, meaning roughly 3.3 years of those earnings would repay its debts if nothing else were paid. It also says its cost of borrowing fell from 10.3% in FY19 to 7.8%. When it needed fresh equity it raised ₹24,930 crore through a rights issue, and the company says it was oversubscribed by 30%. A rights issue offers new shares to existing owners. These are the company's own figures, so read them as its best case.

blocks.text: Rivals, in plain sight

The rival in the headlines is Mukesh Ambani. Adani went from second place back to first on Forbes's India list in 2026, with a $20.7 billion rise that year. In cement he is chasing UltraTech, and he said in 2022 he aimed to be the largest by 2030. In airports he beat GMR in 2019, and lost Jewar to Zurich. In power, Business Today's 2021 comparison with Tata Power showed the gap in valuation and debt.

Our reading: he wins mostly by being willing to pay more and wait longer than others, in sectors where the government hands out licences. When that works, as in airports, he ends up as the largest private operator. When it does not, as in Yangon or Carmichael, he takes the loss or cuts the plan. Now he is making his biggest bet yet: $100 billion toward AI data centres by 2035, with Google's Vizag hub at its centre. Whether it pays is unknown, but the pattern is familiar. __He is again betting that the thing everyone will need is the thing he already controls: land, power and wires.__
Same trick since Mundra: own the boring thing everyone will need.
What he got right and wrong

What he got right: he found one geographic advantage and kept stacking businesses on it. He moved faster than rivals, and he kept his word on deals, and he backed people through expensive mistakes. He turned a lost partner into a port, and in 2023 he chose survival over pride in a matter of days.

What he got wrong: he signed a fixed price on a floating cost and nearly lost his power company. He built an Australian mine that shipped about seven years late, at one-sixth of its planned size. He leased land in Myanmar from a company that later fell under US sanctions. His flagship paid $275 million to settle over Iranian-origin gas, without admitting the allegations. Each time the group was big enough to survive. You will not be, so learn from his costs, not his recoveries.

blocks.title: Own the thing beside the thing
blocks.text: Every Adani business began by looking at what the last one needed. A port needs coal. Coal needs a plant. A plant needs wires. Wires need customers. If you are starting up, ask what your first customers must buy next, and whether you can be the one who sells it.

blocks.title: Make your debt boring before it makes you famous
blocks.text: Part of the fear in 2023 came from share-backed loans. Borrowed money makes your rise faster, and your fall faster too. If a lender can force you to sell at the worst moment, you do not fully control your own company.
The day, in his own words

The most detailed account of Gautam Adani's day did not come from a business magazine. It came from a TV audience. In January 2023, someone on India TV's show Aap Ki Adalat asked how a man with his schedule finds time for family. His answer started with travel: three days a week he is out of Ahmedabad. On the other four he reaches the office at about ==10:30 or 11 am==, because he got home at 11 or midnight the night before.

The mornings are the surprise. He says he wakes at 6:30 and exercises for about an hour. Then he spends ==two to two and a half hours== at the dining table, reading newspapers and talking with his wife, children and granddaughter. He also has a rule for lunch: whichever family members are in the office eat together in the dining room.

items.label: When he says he wakes up, followed by an hour of exercise
Newspapers and family talk at the table, before he leaves for work
Time he says he spends out of Ahmedabad each week
His office day, according to his biographer R.N. Bhaskar and India Today

blocks.text: Notice the order. Body, family, newspapers. Only then the empire.

When he does get to work, he stays there. Bhaskar's 2022 book puts his day at eleven to twelve hours in the office, and India Today's profile says twelve hours on most days. Adani told India Today he does not really separate rest from work.
I always tell people that when I am at work, I relax. Whenever I go on a holiday, I work too.
blocks.who: Gautam Adani to India Today, 2022

blocks.text: In December 2024 India was arguing about Narayana Murthy's 70-hour work week. Adani told the news agency IANS that nobody can set this rule for anyone else. "Your work-life balance should not be imposed on me, and my work-life balance shouldn't be imposed on you," he said. Then came the line that went viral: if you spend eight hours with family, "biwi bhaag jayegi", your wife will run away. The joke got the headlines, but the sentence after it says more: "For us either it is family or work, we don't have a world out of this."
Two worlds, no third. Decide honestly if you want that life.
What he says he does, and what others saw
I do not interfere in the day-to-day functioning of the companies. My role is limited to formulating strategy, capital allocation and performance review.
blocks.who: Gautam Adani to India Today, 2022

blocks.text: He has told this story for a long time. In 2012 he told the Economic Times, "Delegation has never been a problem for me," and said he began handing off operating decisions back when Adani was only a trading firm. His long-time lieutenant Malay Mahadevia added one detail: Adani "reviews the functioning of the businesses every month" to check that the processes are not turning bureaucratic. Bhaskar's book adds another. __He delegates, yet he expects each person to report directly on progress__, and he steps in fast on a go or no-go call when a job gets stuck.

Outsiders describe a tighter grip. Bloomberg editor Anto Antony, who spent nearly two weeks around the family, said he has essentially been the "super CEO", making all the decisions for the conglomerate. Bloomberg also reported, citing officials who were present, that in 2022 he scolded his son Karan before other executives over an unexpected $11 million quarterly loss at ACC. In 2024 he pulled up his son Jeet in a meeting over slow digital plans.

Hindenburg Research, a short seller that stood to profit if the shares fell, quoted unnamed former executives saying that all key decisions flow back to him. Treat that as an interested party's claim. Still, the accounts fit together better than they first appear. __He hands over the running of things. He does not hand over where the money goes.__
Delegate the work. Keep the capital decisions. That is the real split.

For example: the Economic Times retold a story in 2012 that it openly called legend. In the early 1990s a commodities trader lost Adani Enterprises ==₹6 crore== in one day and offered to resign. Adani is believed to have told him, "You have learnt a lot today. Your learning cost me six crore rupees. Now you must stay and earn back that much." The tale goes that the trader did it in six months. We cannot confirm it happened, but it is the story his company chooses to tell about mistakes.
How he hires

In 1997 Adani walked into the Mumbai Port Trust office about some consignments and offered its vice chairman, an IAS officer named Rajeeva Sinha, a job on his planned port at Mundra. Sinha said no, and thought it was a spur-of-the-moment offer. "In 1997, he couldn't get anyone to join him," Sinha recalled later. Adani remembers it differently.
I had done my homework. I had heard Mr Sinha was passionate about ports.
blocks.who: Gautam Adani to the Economic Times, 2012

blocks.text: Sinha joined ten years later as a director of Adani Ports. Back when the port was only a plan, nobody, it seemed, wanted to risk joining an unknown Ahmedabad firm. That was why the job had gone to his childhood friend Malay Mahadevia, then fresh from a dentistry degree. The Economic Times called Mahadevia, in many ways, Adani's alter ego. He is still listed on the group's leadership page, as a director of airports and healthcare.
A dentist helped build Mundra. When no expert will come, pick someone you trust.

His hiring talks can run long. Vneet Jaain, a CEO at Adani Power in 2012 (spelled Vineet Jain in that report), remembered being invited to the Adani guest house in Delhi and discussing the power industry for four hours, until one in the morning. A week later Mahadevia called with the offer. In 2008 Adani told Mint that people were his biggest limit: "Give me people and I would do projects, just like that." That same year he mentioned the Adani Knowledge Centre, which he called a nursery for growing managers.

Not every hire worked. Ravi Sharma ran telecom companies before he became CEO of Adani Power, with no power experience, and he left after about two years. "It took me a year to recruit Ravi, so his departure is quite unfortunate," Adani said, adding that hiring from a totally different field carries a risk. We found no reliable on-record account of how he personally fires people, so we will not guess.
What it is like to work for him

A warning first: most on-record voices are people who worked for him and speak well of him, so read them as friendly witnesses. Vinay Prakash, who joined in 2001, said in 2012, "Gautambhai gives us his dreams and however big they may be, he wants us to achieve them." In 2017 Prakash said the chairman once told him that "your employees would be as loyal to you as you are to them". He also described a culture that lets people take risks, make mistakes and get a second chance.

Jaain told the Economic Times he is a fan but not a flatterer: "I disagree and argue with him." He said Adani answers email and SMS very quickly even when away. Then he gave the most useful advice anyone has given about this man.
You have to be very direct and to-the-point when you communicate with Gautambhai. He's got a very short attention span.
blocks.who: Vneet Jaain, then CEO at Adani Power, 2012

blocks.text: Lead with your one line. Every investor you pitch will thank you.

There is a softer route too. Prakash said he called Adani's brother Rajesh more often than Gautam: "Rajeshbhai is softer, less aggressive." Then-CFO Dewang Desai said executives consult the brothers on issues they might not want to take to Gautam's level. So the family works as a kind of shock absorber between the boss and his managers.

Retired communications head Devendra Amin told Bhaskar: "A lack of formal education allows him to think out of the box and make swift decisions." India Today says he follows his gut and prefers simple solutions. His wife Priti says that once he picks a topic, he cannot rest until he knows everything about it. And his top people can out-earn him: in FY25 his Adani Enterprises resources CEO Vinay Prakash received ==₹69.34 crore==, while Adani himself drew ==₹10.41 crore==.

The structure keeps changing. In 2012 the group employed about 12,000 people. By June 2026 Adani said nearly 400,000 people were associated with its operations, about 85% of them at sites and plants, and he announced a move to just three management layers at headquarters and project sites. His stated reason was less bureaucracy and sharper accountability. __The bigger a company gets, the harder its founder must fight to keep the org chart small.__

Anyone can print values on a wall. What matters is what a person does when the value costs something. Here are eight beliefs Adani keeps repeating, each with a real moment beside it. Some moments flatter him. Some are more complicated, and we say so.
1. There is no shortcut, so stop looking for one

On Aap Ki Adalat the host asked him for his formula for making money. He said there is no maths, chemistry or physics to it, only "hard work, hard work and hard work". The host then mentioned a story from his friends: that while the Mundra land was being developed, he got up at 4 am and went there daily. He did not deny it, and he shared the credit.
The success of any man depends on honesty and hard work, and the rest is left to God; that's the only formula.
blocks.who: Gautam Adani, Aap Ki Adalat, January 2023

blocks.text: 2. Do not carry what you cannot control

He has been held for ransom and trapped in a terror attack, and we tell those stories in the next chapter. What is striking is what he says about the nights after them. "I was kidnapped and released the next day," he told the same show. "I tell you, that I slept well that very night." He told India Today that even on traumatic days he sleeps peacefully.
When things are not in your control, why worry? Destiny decides such things.
blocks.who: Gautam Adani to India Today, 2022

blocks.text: Most founders lose more sleep than money. Practise this one early.
3. Your word is worth more than your legal right

He says his father's rule was that a promise must always be kept. The group's biggest test of this came on 1 February 2023. Adani Enterprises had just closed a ==₹20,000 crore== share sale, fully subscribed, and it could legally have kept the money. But the stock had crashed well below the offer price, so the board returned the cash. In August 2026 he called this the clearest expression of his philosophy.
Trust is greater than any legal right.
blocks.who: Gautam Adani to Adani Group staff, August 2026

blocks.text: Be fair about the other side of it. Keeping the money would have meant investors holding shares at more than double the market price, as PTI noted, and that would have done its own damage. __So this was both a principled move and a smart one.__ The two often go together, and that does not make it less real.
4. Build what your country is short of

He says the idea came from growing up in the 1970s and 80s, when people had to struggle for basic services. He watched China, which he notes had a lower per capita income in 1990, leap ahead on infrastructure while India waited. When the 1991 reforms opened the door to private players, he went through it.
I was born in a middle-class family and I lived through the 1970s and 80s when we had to struggle for bijli, sadak and paani.
blocks.who: Gautam Adani to India Today, December 2022

blocks.text: He also treats this as strategy. Aligning with national aims, he says, "gives our activities the required tailwind that makes for smooth sailing". Critics hear something else: a business empire that rises along with one political leader. His companies and the Modi government have consistently denied favouritism. Both things can be true of the same strategy, and we look at this again in the chapter on his public image.
5. Connect the dots

His favourite word is "adjacencies", and the chain is easy to follow once you see it. The Mundra port brought in coal, and coal plus Mundra's land led to power. Power led to transmission and renewables. Bringing in edible oil for Wilmar led to a 50:50 venture. And cement came next, because power plants produce fly ash that cement can use as feedstock.
Do not ask what is hot. Ask what your last business makes possible.
6. Know the limit of your risk, then jump

He says diamonds taught him this as a teenager, with no safety net, and Bhaskar's book tells a story from those years. Young Gautam sold ==₹1.5 lakh== of stones on a spoken promise, told nobody in the office, and went home on holiday. The trader then stopped answering calls. So Gautam and his cousin Girish went to the man's house at 6 am, arriving when the milk boy rang the bell, and left with other stones in settlement. They made very little money on the deal.
In this field, hesitation is the difference between winning and losing.
blocks.who: Gautam Adani, Jaipur, November 2024

blocks.text: A young trader's nerve is not the same as a plan, and he knows it. "When you take risks, you need to know its limit," he told the same TV audience, adding that he has failed in many places too. He added a harder idea in Jaipur: "Too much of an attachment to outcomes limits your ability to challenge the status quo." __Bold on the decision, calm about the result.__
7. Scrutiny is the price of big dreams

Ten days after US prosecutors' charges became public, he stood up at a jewellery awards night in Jaipur. He listed his crises like a scorecard: the Australian mine, the short seller, the US case. "Every attack makes us stronger," he said. In June 2026 he told shareholders, "We did not bend. We did not pause."
The more bold your dreams, the more the world will scrutinize you.
blocks.who: Gautam Adani, Jaipur, November 2024

blocks.text: Take this belief carefully. It works when the critics are wrong and it blinds you when they are right. To his credit, in August 2026 he also thanked those who questioned the group, saying criticism of any intent offers a chance for introspection. In the "what went wrong" chapter you will see a case where ignoring early warnings cost $275 million.
Some critics are noise. Some are your free audit. Learn to tell them apart.
8. Wisdom needs knowledge too

This one is for every student reading. Asked by the TV host if dropping out was the secret, he said no, firmly. He called education very important and said missing it was his misfortune. His own formula is plain: "While education equips you with knowledge, it's life's experiences that give you wisdom. Knowledge combined with wisdom ensures success."
I sometimes wonder that had I had the education along with this hard work and experience, then I would've become much bigger than the current Gautam Adani.
blocks.who: Gautam Adani, Aap Ki Adalat, January 2023

blocks.text: An audience member said many people want to become like him. His reply is worth copying down. Find what actually interests you and follow it, he said: "You should have the liking for it, not like I saw him, I want to become like him."
The man himself says do not copy him. Read that again.
Two people he credits

India Today calls him the seventh of eight children. In a LinkedIn post in March 2026, he wrote about his mother, Shantaben, telling him stories from the Ramayana as a child, including that of Kaushalya, who had to let her son go. He said he understood it only later, after leaving home for Mumbai at 16 with almost nothing. "My mother let me go," he wrote.

He married Priti on ==1 May 1986==, a marriage arranged by two families with business ties. She had trained as a dentist. She stepped away from practice and later came to lead the Adani Foundation. He calls her his "Lady Luck", and he likes to joke about the gap between them: "She is more qualified than me–I am just a 10th pass and she is a doctor."
If my mother gave me my values, my wife Priti has been the keeper of my conscience.
blocks.who: Gautam Adani, International Women's Day post, March 2026

blocks.text: He told TV viewers that Priti works seven to eight hours a day on the foundation. He has said that every evening she tells him at least one story of a life it has touched. On their 40th wedding anniversary, 1 May 2026, the two of them went to Kedarnath to pray that morning, and he told his staff about it in a speech the same day.

They have two sons, Karan and Jeet, both now senior in the group. He has written publicly about three granddaughters who call him "Dadu". His younger brother Rajesh and his nephews Pranav and Sagar also work in the business. We have left the grandchildren's lives out, beyond the family's own mention of them.
The evening he was kidnapped

On the evening of ==1 January 1998==, Adani and an associate, Shantilal Patel, drove away from Ahmedabad's Karnavati Club. According to court papers and press reports, a scooter stopped their car, and armed men forced both into another vehicle. They were blindfolded and held in a room. Police alleged the kidnappers sought ==₹15 crore==, and the charge sheet says the two were released.

Nobody was convicted. A court acquitted six accused in 2005 for lack of evidence, and in November 2018 acquitted the last two accused, giving them the benefit of the doubt. Adani did not appear to testify in that final trial. He asked the court to rely on the statement he had given in the earlier one, and the prosecution dropped him from its witness list. What he remembers is his reaction: he says he slept well the very night he got home.
A ₹15 crore kidnap demand, and his stated takeaway is: forget it fast.
Fifteen feet at the Taj

On ==26 November 2008== he was at the Taj Mahal Hotel in Mumbai, dining at Masala Craft with Mohammed Sharaf, the CEO of DP World. He says they had paid the bill five minutes before and were about to leave, but his friend wanted to keep talking over coffee. Business Today's account, published within weeks, says he then saw gunmen firing in the lobby from about 15 feet away. If he had left on time, he says, he would have been in that lobby.

The lights went out and staff moved diners to the kitchen, where he spent two hours. Priti called from Ahmedabad to warn him that news channels were reporting an attack in Colaba, and he told her he was trapped inside. Staff then led guests through service passages to a hotel lounge called The Chambers, where he spent the next ten hours. At 4 am a grenade blast close by brought the panic back.

National Security Guard commandos reached the group at dawn and walked about 150 guests out by around 8:30 am. He flew home to Ahmedabad on his private jet and found his extended family at the house, bleary-eyed after watching it all on television. He has never forgotten who saved him: years later he praised the dedication of Taj staff, down to the waiters, as very rare in organisations today.
I saw death at a distance of just 15ft.
blocks.who: Gautam Adani to reporters in Ahmedabad, 2008, as quoted by the BBC

blocks.text: He credits the waiters. Ask who would save your customers on your worst night.
How he spends his time and money

His stress relief is close to comic for one of Asia's richest men. Many nights he plays rummy paplu with Priti, 8 to 10 games on his telling, and India Today says it happens three or four times a week. "This is a secret," he told viewers. "I play 8-10 games, and most of the time she wins." He says he ends up owing her money.

India Today's profile fills in the rest. He shuns parties. He says he does not have many friends, and likes walking and exercising alone. He loves old Hindi songs by Mukesh and Kishore Kumar, is a vegetarian, enjoys Gujarati food, and lists Switzerland as his favourite getaway. Massive paintings line his office walls, yet he admits he cannot recall half the artists' names.
Billions in the bank. Favourite evening: cards with his wife.

items.label: His total pay in FY25, from two of nine listed group companies. Less than most peers
What one of his own CEOs, Vinay Prakash, received that same year
Private jets he owns for business travel, per India Today, plus a fleet of luxury cars

blocks.text: The modest pay needs context. Like other promoters he also earns from dividends. India Today reports that he owns four private jets, and that he still prefers a black bulletproof Toyota Alphard with a convoy of bodyguards for the office run. Former group CFO Ameet Desai told Mint he helped set up a family office, with a separate team managing the family's private investments, kept apart from the listed companies.

Money, he says, is not the point: you "can't chew on money", and he prefers the thrill of hard problems. Whether you believe that is up to you. India Today's writers add a sharper reading, that he understands money ultimately means power, both to keep his family secure and to influence others.
Giving

Two big gifts have been tied to family dates. In June 2022, when he turned 60, the family set aside ==₹60,000 crore== for health, education and skills work through the Adani Foundation. In February 2025, his son Jeet married Diva Shah in what was described as a small ceremony in Ahmedabad, with politicians and celebrities notably absent. Reports at the time said he would give another ==₹10,000 crore== to social causes, plus ₹10 lakh each to 500 newly married women with disabilities every year.

He says the foundation now works in 22 Indian states and has touched more than 10 million lives. We should be straight about the limits here: those figures and the wedding details come from the group, from him, or from NDTV, which the group owns. __A pledge is not the same as money spent__, and we did not find an independent audit of how much of these sums has been deployed so far.
Check who is telling you the good news. Then keep reading anyway.

We also searched for his health. We found no reliable public reporting of health struggles, so we will not discuss the subject. The people who matter to him, on his own telling, are few. "I have always lived between two worlds, work and family," he wrote in 2026. "And everything I have built in the first world was made possible because of the strength I draw from the second."

chapters.title: The Quiet Man Everyone Argues About

blocks.text: From invisible to inescapable

For most of his career Adani's brand was that he had no brand. The BBC noted in 2022 that he often describes himself as low-profile and rarely talks about the crises of his life, apart from once telling a journalist that "two or three very unfortunate incidents have happened in my life". Bloomberg's editor said that until 2023 many saw the group as opaque, with little known about how it worked inside.

The group wrapped itself in a single idea instead of one man's personality: "Nation Building" and "Growth with Goodness". Those phrases are the guiding philosophy on its website, and they appear in almost everything it publishes. His own speeches take the same tone. He rarely sells a product. He talks about India's century and his part in it.
Sell the mission, not yourself. Then see what happens when the mission gets questioned.
The courtroom on TV

Then in January 2023 he did something very unlike him. He sat in the hot seat on Aap Ki Adalat, a show styled as a courtroom, and took questions on Rahul Gandhi, Modi, bank loans and his wealth for a mass Hindi audience. The host threw jokes and he joked back. Asked about Rahul Gandhi's attacks, he said, "During the 2014 elections and post that, Rahul ji has continuously attacked me, because of which you all know who I am."

Those were also the moments that aged the worst. The host said that some people believe all the banks will go bust if the Adani bubble bursts. "Some people have such a dream," he answered, and said his assets were three to four times his loans. Would the balloon keep flying? His reply is below.
This balloon will keep flying as long as India is progressing.
blocks.who: Gautam Adani, Aap Ki Adalat, January 2023

blocks.text: On ==24 January 2023==, a little over two weeks after that show, Hindenburg published the report that wiped more than $100 billion off his companies within days. We tell that story in the next chapter. The timing shows you something, though. __Never make your public image rest on a metaphor your critics can pop.__
About two weeks. That is how fast a public story can flip.
How he talks now

Bloomberg's editor says that after Hindenburg the group turned "very aggressive about communicating" with investors and media. Group companies held investor road shows and calls with bondholders. And Adani's own voice got more personal. He wrote long LinkedIn essays about his mother, his wife and his granddaughters. In October 2026 he posted a long reflection after meeting Michael Bloomberg in Delhi.

In May 2026 he started an internal address series called "Apni Baat, Apno Ke Saath", or roughly "our talk, among our own". The first one told the Ramayana story of a squirrel rolling in wet sand to help build Ram's bridge, as a lesson that no worker's contribution is too small. The second drew on the Samudra Manthan, the churning of the ocean, to talk about the US case. Note how he frames the group as a family, the "Adani Parivar". __He is a storyteller, and his stories come from the epics, not from Silicon Valley.__

He is also short and blunt when it suits him. His June 2026 AGM speech ran ==35 minutes==, against ==2.5 hours== for Mukesh Ambani's days earlier, as Mint pointed out. Mint added that he gave no capex guidance for the current year. __Your image is shaped by what you leave out too.__
Buying a microphone

In 2022 he stepped into news media in a big way. In August a group company indirectly acquired a 29% stake in NDTV, a move the NDTV founders said happened without their consent. By December 2022 he was set to control ==64.71%== after the founders agreed to sell most of their shares. He told the Financial Times this was a "responsibility" rather than a business opportunity, and he said he wanted a global Indian outlet to match the FT or Al Jazeera.
Independence means if government has done something wrong, you say it's wrong. But at the same time, you should have courage when the government is doing the right thing every day.
blocks.who: Gautam Adani to the Financial Times, November 2022, as reported by Reuters

blocks.text: Critics read that second sentence as a warning. NDTV anchor Ravish Kumar resigned around the takeover and told Foreign Policy he was asking whether the government had the courage to face criticism. Be aware of this as you read: several of the speeches and stories in this book reached us through NDTV, a news group he now controls, and we have tried to flag where that matters.
How India sees him

In India he is not one thing. To admirers he is a first-generation builder. He leans on that image when he says he knows the mindset of the person on a scooter, a rickshaw or a bus. India Today named him its Newsmaker of the Year 2022. Rajiv Jain of GQG, while investing in 2023, called him "widely regarded as among the best entrepreneurs of his generation".

To critics he is the prime example of crony capitalism. The Financial Times notes that when Narendra Modi took office in 2014, he flew from Gujarat to Delhi in Adani's private jet, an open display of friendship. Forbes, in its own summary, says he grew partly by cultivating close ties to Modi. The Congress party has a slogan for it: "Aam Aadmi Behaal, Adani maalamaal", the common man in ruin, Adani in riches.

His answers are worth knowing, whichever way you lean. He says one "cannot take personal help from Modi ji", that policies apply to everyone, and that he works with opposition-run states such as Kerala and West Bengal too. He says nothing is won without a bid: "The Adani Group has a philosophy that nothing should be touched without a bid." His biographer R.N. Bhaskar puts it more bluntly: "He's close to every politician that is in power."
Politics can give you a tailwind. It also hands your rivals a headline.
How the world sees him

Abroad, the name often meets a protest before it meets a customer. In Australia, activists fought the Carmichael coal mine for seven years, and their pressure scared off lenders, insurers and engineering firms. In November 2020 the local unit renamed itself ==Bravus==, saying it came from the Latin for brave. The Guardian then reported that Latin experts said it was closer to "crooked" or "mercenary". The company said the name was derived from "brave" or "bold", and it denied the rebrand had anything to do with controversy.

In Kenya, plans to run Nairobi's main airport for 30 years were hugely unpopular, as the BBC put it, and led airport workers to strike in September 2024. President Ruto cancelled the plan and a power-line deal after the US charges. In Sri Lanka, a new government wanted lower prices on two wind projects, and Adani withdrew in February 2025, calling them financially unviable. In Bangladesh, Adani Power has fought over unpaid power bills, and in November 2025 a court there paused the arbitration until a review of the contract is done.

Norway's giant wealth fund has its own view. Its public exclusion list names Adani Ports, for risk of contributing to rights violations in war or conflict, and since February 2026 Adani Green Energy, under "gross corruption or other serious financial crime". The fund gave no further detail on the Green decision. As of the list's update dated 11 August 2026, both names were still there. Meanwhile, investors such as GQG Partners of the US have bought in since the crisis, and Google has signed up for a data centre in Visakhapatnam.

For example: a founder's name can become a campaign. In Australia the fight over one mine turned his surname into a protest slogan, #StopAdani, and his own company ended up changing the name on its door. In India the same surname marks one end of a cricket pitch, a right he says was simply bought. "A stadium is made with an auction," he told the TV audience.

chapters.title: What Went Wrong, and What It Cost

blocks.text: Read this chapter slowly and precisely. Adani has been accused of many things and has denied them, and several high-profile cases have ended without any finding of guilt. Others ended in settlements, where people pay without admitting or denying. __A young reader should learn to tell apart an allegation, a settlement, a regulator's finding and a conviction.__ Each is different, and we keep them separate below.

items.text: SEBI bars promoter entities of Adani Exports from the market for two years over the Ketan Parekh matter.
The appeal ends in a paid consent settlement, approved by the appellate tribunal.
Karnataka's Lokayukta report accuses Adani Enterprises of bribery at Belekeri port. The group says the case closed in its favour in 2017.
Hindenburg publishes its report. The group denies it. About $150 billion of market value goes at the worst point.
US prosecutors charge Adani with fraud offences. He denies wrongdoing.
SEBI's orders find the allegations it examined not established.
Adani Enterprises pays $275 million to settle Iran sanctions liability. SEC settlements follow.
A US judge dismisses the criminal case with prejudice, while calling the process concerning.

blocks.text: The first brush: the market ban

In May 2007, SEBI ruled on trading in Adani Exports shares from 1999 to 2001. It found that promoter entities had aided and abetted firms linked to Ketan Parekh, the market operator at the centre of that scam, in manipulating the stock. It barred seven promoter entities from the market for two years. The promoters' defence was that they sold shares to raise money for Mundra and did not know who was buying. SEBI said the same buyers on nearly every share could not be a coincidence.

The tribunal stayed the ban after about 50 days, and in April 2008 the case ended through consent terms: one entity paid ₹10.5 lakh and others ₹7.5 lakh each. Within a week the group filed papers for the Adani Power share sale. Hindenburg later described the outcome as bans reduced to token fines, and the group says the matter was closed and disclosed. You can read that in two ways: a clean exit or a cheap one. Either way, the shadow followed him for 15 years.
A cheap settlement in 2008 can still be a headline in 2023.
The Belekeri allegations

In July 2011 Karnataka's anti-corruption ombudsman, the Lokayukta headed by Justice Hegde, published its report on illegal mining. It said Adani Enterprises had paid bribes for undue favour in exporting iron ore through Belekeri port, and it recommended blacklisting the firm. The group's own later account is that a special investigation team found the allegations false, filed a closure report, and that a Lokayukta court accepted it in July 2017. That closure detail rests on the company's document, so we report it as its account.
The coal mine that swallowed a decade

He bought the Carmichael project in Queensland in 2010, planning up to 60 million tonnes a year. Activists fought it for seven years, and lenders, insurers and engineering firms walked away. The first cargo shipped only in December 2021, from a mine with capacity for 10 million tonnes. He calls it a sign of resilience. Then in Jaipur in 2024, he gave a rare honest number about what it cost.
The fact is that 100% equity funding took away over 30 billion dollars of debt financing from our green energy projects.
blocks.who: Gautam Adani, Jaipur, November 2024

blocks.text: He says the mine took about ==$10 billion== of the group's own equity. That is his framing and his sum, and the activists would tell the story very differently. There is also a complaint on file: Reuters reported in 2024 that an Aboriginal group filed a complaint with Australia's Human Rights Commission accusing the coal unit of racism. __When a project gets too hot for lenders, the real bill arrives in the projects you can no longer fund.__
The short seller and the share sale

On 24 January 2023 Hindenburg Research accused the group of "the largest con in corporate history", alleging stock manipulation and accounting fraud through offshore entities. It also said it had taken a position that would profit if the shares fell, and the group called the report baseless. The timing was brutal, as Adani Enterprises was in the middle of a ₹20,000 crore share sale. By 2 February the group had lost about ==$108 billion== in market value, and his own fortune was down by tens of billions.
For me, the interest of my investors is paramount and everything is secondary.
blocks.who: Gautam Adani, video message, 2 February 2023

blocks.text: What happened next is worth studying: the sale's proceeds went back. Group promoters prepaid ==$2.15 billion== of share-backed loans in about six weeks, plus $500 million of Ambuja acquisition debt. They sold ==$1.87 billion== of stock to the US investor GQG Partners. They slowed acquisitions and made hard choices on capex, and Business Today reported net debt to EBITDA falling to 3.27 times from 3.81. Reuters reported that the shares have since recovered.
Loans against your own shares make a bad week far more dangerous.

Then the verdicts, which need care. In January 2024 the Supreme Court disposed of the petitions and told SEBI to finish its last two probes. On 18 September 2025, two SEBI orders found that the charges they examined, about money routed through three companies, were not established. All the loans were repaid with interest, and at that time the law did not count such indirect deals as related-party transactions.

Reuters headlined this as SEBI dismissing the allegations. The Indian Express also pointed out what the orders did not address: low public float, foreign portfolio investors and the offshore links of his brother Vinod Adani. An earlier Supreme Court panel had found no conclusive evidence of price manipulation but flagged opacity around such investors.

So be careful with the phrase "clean chit". It is accurate for the charges decided, and less clearly so for everything Hindenburg alleged. Hindenburg itself shut down in January 2025, and the group's shares went on to recover.
The US case

In November 2024 US prosecutors charged him, his nephew Sagar and six others over an alleged scheme to pay about ==$265 million== in bribes to Indian state officials for solar contracts, and to hide it from American investors. Arrest warrants were issued for him and Sagar. The group called the claims baseless. It also pointed out that he faced three fraud-related counts and was not charged in the count of conspiring to violate the US foreign bribery law. The Hindu noted that the indictment still names him in describing the alleged scheme.

The damage was immediate. Adani Green dropped a $600 million bond, and Kenya scrapped deals worth over $2.5 billion. TotalEnergies paused new investments and said it had not been told of the investigation, which is a painful thing for a partner to say in public. Sri Lanka began reviewing its projects, and Norway's fund later excluded Adani Green. Adani himself never appeared in a US court.
Notice who moved first: partners and lenders, long before any court.

Then the US government changed its mind. In May 2026, after Adani hired a legal team led by Sullivan & Cromwell's Robert Giuffra, who is also a personal lawyer to President Trump, the Justice Department asked to drop the case. Judge Nicholas Garaufis first refused to accept a "terse, bland, and conclusory" request. The department replied that the alleged conduct was centred in India, that no investor had lost money, and that the case "should have been dropped a year ago -- or never brought in the first place".

On ==10 August 2026== the judge dismissed the charges with prejudice, meaning they cannot be brought again. His 47-page order examined whether Adani's $10 billion US investment pledge had played a role, and concluded it had not. But he said a senior official appeared to have acted without meaningful input from the prosecutors and investigators who built the case. Adani said he accepted the result with humility, and that his faith in the rule of law remained unwavering.
The irregularities in the decision to dismiss the indictment are concerning.
blocks.who: US District Judge Nicholas Garaufis, order of 10 August 2026, as quoted by the BBC

blocks.text: Be exact about what this means. __No court ever ruled on whether the bribery happened, in either direction.__ A separate civil case ended the same day with a consent judgment: he pays ==$6 million== and Sagar ==$12 million==, without admitting or denying the allegations, and both are barred from future violations of certain US securities laws.
Dismissed is not disproved, and settled is not guilty. Learn these words.
The cargo no one questioned

This one is smaller and more instructive, because it reads like a textbook. In 2023 Adani Enterprises entered the Indian LPG market. Facing strong rivals, it needed discounted gas, and a Dubai trader offered it, said to be from Oman and Iraq. According to the US Treasury, the gas was actually Iranian, and from November 2023 to June 2025 the company bought 35 cargoes, with 32 payments totalling about ==$192 million== going through US banks.

For example: look at the warning signs the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control lists. The first cargo was refrigerated propane said to be loaded at Sohar, Oman, where no facility for exporting it existed at the time. Certificates of origin had illogical numbering. Ships switched off their tracking or faked their location. Third parties raised concerns about Iranian origin at least four times. And the price looked too good, in a region where Iran, almost alone, sold at such a discount.

On 18 May 2026 the company agreed to pay ==$275 million==, against a legal maximum of about $384 million. Treasury called the apparent violations egregious and not voluntarily disclosed, while crediting remedial steps and cooperation. The company's checks did find no sanctioned names, and none of its documents explicitly showed Iranian origin. The settlement itself contains no finding of fault. But the lesson is simple, and it is expensive: __a checklist is not the same as curiosity.__

blocks.text: Fighting the critics

There is one more fight a young founder should think about. In September 2025 Adani Enterprises won a one-sided court order restraining five journalists and unknown others from publishing what the judge called "unverified, unsubstantiated" and defamatory reports. The company had argued they were aligned with "anti-India interests". The government then sent takedown notices. On appeal, one judge set the order aside for four journalists, and another said the fifth need not follow it until he was heard.

He may feel wronged, and courts exist for that. But a giant company asking a court to silence reporters rarely looks like strength. This is our view, not a legal finding. __You win more trust by publishing the answer than by removing the question.__
What not to copy

Here is our own list, drawn from the record above. Do not borrow against your own shares, because a falling price then turns into a margin call on your life. Do not let one political relationship become your whole public story. Do not treat a compliance team as a box to tick.

Do not leave partners to learn about your legal trouble from the papers, as TotalEnergies said it did. And do not assume an expensive legal team will rescue you. Most founders will never have that option.

As of November 2026 Gautam Adani is 64 and chairman of the Adani Group, with four younger relatives taking on more of the operations. Forbes put him back at ==No. 1== on its India's 100 Richest list that came out on 1 October, up $20.7 billion to ==$112.7 billion== which he shares with his family. Mukesh Ambani fell to second place at $86.3 billion. Forbes also noted that his fortune is still below the $150 billion peak he hit in 2022.

blocks.text: What he is betting on

The theme he repeats now is that infrastructure and intelligence are becoming one business. In his May 2026 letter to shareholders he summed it up in one line: "Before AI can think, energy must flow." So the plan is to supply the things AI needs. Forbes says the group is investing $100 billion in AI infrastructure. At the June 2026 AGM he named a 3 GW data centre platform by 2030 and a gigawatt-scale Google campus in Visakhapatnam.

Then the rest of the list, at his usual scale. He is targeting ==10 GW== of nuclear power by 2035 through a new company, Adani Atomic Energy, which is more than the 8 GW India has today. He wants 45 GW of Adani Power capacity within five years, 5,000 MW of hydropower with Bhutan, and one billion tonnes a year through Adani Ports by 2030. He also has an aerospace and defence push. In October 2026 Adani Enterprises reported its best half-year ever, with EBITDA up 56% to ₹11,958 crore.

The numbers go further still. In October 2026 CFO Robbie Singh said he wants the group able to invest up to ==$100 billion a year== by 2033, and that 72% of forward capex now comes from its own cash flow. "India is a tremendous opportunity and it is for us to lose," Singh said. "And I do not want to lose." __That dependence on its own cash, not on pledged shares, is the clearest sign of what 2023 taught them.__
₹2 lakh crore this year. The 2033 goal: nearly five times that.
The project he says is closest to him

The one he talks about differently is Dharavi, Mumbai's huge informal settlement, home to about a million people. In his May 2026 speech he called it perhaps among the most challenging tasks of his life and the one closest to his heart. "We did not make this decision for the sake of profit," he told staff, calling Dharavi a symbol of "our collective failure". Hold him to that line as the project progresses. It runs through a company with the Maharashtra government as co-shareholder, and the first test is whether residents end up better off.

Work has begun. In mid-October 2026 a bhoomi poojan marked the start of rehabilitation construction at a 22-acre railway site in Matunga, with 10 towers and 10,432 homes due in phases by August 2030. Pranav Adani told Fortune India the plan is about 200,000 houses in total and $4–5 billion in the first phase. Meeting Michael Bloomberg that month, Adani wrote that Dharavi should be judged on housing, sanitation, electricity and residents' economic security.
After the storm

His tone in 2026 has been part victory lap and part sermon. He called the ₹25,000 crore rights issue in Adani Enterprises "a referendum on our credibility", and told shareholders, "We built when it was hardest to build." In August, days after the US dismissal, he told more than three lakh staff and partners that the experience left him with humility rather than triumph. He asked them what their generation will be remembered for.

The legal cloud has lifted but the questions have not all gone. The judge's concerns are on the record, Norway's exclusion list still carried his companies in August, and Bangladesh's dispute was unresolved at last report. At the same time, money keeps coming. He tops Forbes' India list and is building faster than ever. Whether that is vindication or just survival is an argument people in India will keep having for years.
A closed case is not the same as a settled argument.
What he says he wants next

The clearest answer is about leaving. In early 2018 he invited his sons Karan and Jeet and his nephews Pranav and Sagar to lunch and asked if they wanted to split the group and part ways. He gave them three months. They came back and said they would stay together. Today, Bloomberg reports, four heirs split the businesses and even shared services such as HR and finance, with no first among equals, once he steps down at 70.
Succession is not a one-off event but it is a long term journey. And my plan of succession started almost a decade ago.
blocks.who: Gautam Adani to Bloomberg, 2024

blocks.text: Not everyone is convinced. Wharton professor Raphael Amit told Bloomberg that having no clear leader could become a drawback, unless there are well-defined roles and processes for resolving conflict. That is the real open question of his final chapter. He ended his August 2026 address by calling for institutions that outlast individuals. __The hardest thing he will ever build is a company that does not need him.__
He asked at 55, not 75. Start your succession thinking absurdly early.

lessons.title: Do your homework before the handshake.
lessons.text: In 1997 he offered a port job to Rajeeva Sinha, who assumed it was an impulse. It wasn't. Adani had already learned that Sinha loved ports and feared being transferred away from them, so he offered what the man really wanted.

lessons.title: Hire for trust when you cannot hire for experience.
lessons.text: When no experienced person would risk joining Mundra, he asked a childhood friend who was a newly qualified dentist. Malay Mahadevia learned the job and stayed for decades. Skills can be learned, and character mostly cannot.

lessons.title: Delegate the work, keep the capital.
lessons.text: By his own account his job is strategy, capital allocation and performance review. His monthly business reviews keep him close while CEOs run operations. Early on, decide which decisions only you can make, and hand off the rest.

lessons.title: Get to the point.
lessons.text: Vneet Jaain's advice to future Adani CEOs was to be very direct, because the boss has "a very short attention span". Most powerful people are the same. Put your one best line first, whether in an email, a pitch or a meeting.

lessons.title: Protect your mornings.
lessons.text: With one of the world's largest fortunes, he says he still gives two hours or more each morning to exercise, newspapers and family before reaching office. Then he works late. Decide what comes first, or your calendar will decide for you.

lessons.title: Do not lose sleep over what you cannot control.
lessons.text: He says he slept well the night he came home from a 1998 kidnapping, and that he does not get worked up even on traumatic days. You will rarely face anything close to that. Save your energy for what you can actually change.

lessons.title: Thank the people who save you.
lessons.text: Trapped at the Taj on 26/11, he was led to safety by waiters and staff, and he still praises their dedication years later. Your culture shows on the worst night, not on a poster. Build the kind of team that would do the same for your customers.

lessons.title: Connect the dots from what you already own.
lessons.text: A port brought coal, coal and land led to power, and power plants' fly ash fed into cement. He calls these adjacencies. Before chasing the hot new sector, ask what your last business has made easy for you.

lessons.title: Stay in school if you possibly can.
lessons.text: The most famous dropout in Indian business told a national TV audience that missing his education was his misfortune. He said he might have been much bigger with it. Do not use his story as your excuse.

lessons.title: Give the money back when it feels wrong.
lessons.text: In February 2023 he returned a fully subscribed ₹20,000 crore share sale after the stock crashed. It hurt then, and he now calls it the clearest proof of his values. Keeping your word in a bad week buys more trust than any advertisement.

lessons.title: Never let your shares become your collateral.
lessons.text: After Hindenburg, promoters rushed to prepay $2.15 billion of share-backed loans in about six weeks to remove the risk of margin calls. A loan against your own stock can turn a falling price into a fight for survival. Borrow against cash flow instead.

lessons.title: If the deal looks too cheap, ask why.
lessons.text: Adani Enterprises bought discounted gas with clean-looking papers, and paid $275 million to settle when the US Treasury concluded it was Iranian. The red flags were the price, the ships and the documents. A checklist is not a substitute for curiosity.

lessons.title: Tell your partners first.
lessons.text: When the US charges landed in 2024, TotalEnergies paused new investments and said publicly that it had not been told of the investigation. Bad news ages badly. Your partners should hear it from you, and quickly.

lessons.title: Don't confuse a dismissed case with a clean record.
lessons.text: His US criminal case ended with prejudice in August 2026, yet the judge wrote that the process was concerning and no court ever ruled on the facts. A win on paper does not end the public question. Build a record that does not need a lawyer to explain it.

lessons.title: Plan your exit while you are still strong.
lessons.text: He sat his sons and nephews down in 2018, in his fifties, and gave them three months to decide whether to stay together. Most founders avoid that talk until it is too late. Ask early what your company looks like without you.

factCheck.method: Four writers worked in parallel from primary documents (SEBI, tribunal and US court orders, the US Treasury's OFAC release, prospectuses and annual reports), his own speeches and established press; a separate checker then re-read the merged book, machine-matched every quote and number against the text of its cited sources, opened and read the misses by hand, and checked contacts against the organisations' own pages and photo licences against the Commons API. That check corrected quotes, dates, attributions and net-worth figures and removed one non-free photo. Many Reuters pages, AP and a few others block automated reading, so they were seen only as opening summaries or in other outlets' copies; R.N. Bhaskar's biography was read only in excerpts, Bloomberg's holdings come from data embedded in its public profile page, Vande Bharatam's contacts from its site's footer code, and photos were checked from Commons metadata because image downloads were rate-limited on the check day. Figures are as of the dates given, up to 2 November 2026, and company documents and NDTV, which the group owns, are treated as the group's own voice.

disputed.claim: The 1998 kidnapping: ransom, length and date
disputed.note: PTI and The Indian Express date it to 1 January 1998, and Bloomberg's profile says 1997. Police alleged a Rs 15 crore demand. Outlook Business reports USD 1.5-2 million and says it is not known whether anything was paid, while BBC Hindi quotes a former officer claiming Rs 5 crore. Adani says he was released the next day, and BBC Hindi says he reached home two days after the abduction. Everyone tried was acquitted, so we state no payment. On his absence from the last trial, the BBC says he never turned up, while PTI and TOI say he asked the court to rely on his earlier testimony; we use the latter.

Business Today (2008) has him at Masala Craft, then two hours in the kitchen, then The Chambers lounge. Business Standard (2010) says the Chambers restaurant and about two hours in the dark. India Today (2022) and the BBC mention a basement. Exit time is about 8:30 am in Business Today and 7:30-8 am on his TV account. Bloomberg's profile calls him a hostage. We follow Business Today, the closest to the event.

disputed.claim: Which index ranked him world's second-richest
disputed.note: CBS (via WTOP) and Outlook Business cite Bloomberg's index, about $146.8-147 billion, September 2022. Search excerpts say Forbes's real-time list also placed him second, near $153-154 billion, but we could not open a page to confirm it, so we cite Bloomberg's.

disputed.claim: When the US criminal case ended
disputed.note: Indian outlets, and Fortune India and Business Standard in June, wrote that the case closed in May 2026, when the Justice Department moved to drop it. The court record shows the judge first refused and dismissed the counts against Gautam Adani, Sagar Adani and Vneet Jaain only on 10 August 2026. Counts against five others stayed open, and the appeal over them was still pending in early November 2026.

His own words are that he gave up education at 16 and moved to Mumbai. On Aap Ki Adalat, as ThePrint reports, he said he started work at 15 after Class 10, and India Today also says he left after Class 10. Forbes calls him a college dropout, Bhaskar's book says he left a South Mumbai college within six months, The Times of India says he joined a Mumbai college, The Economic Times (2012) says he left in his second year, and Study International says he left a Gujarat University B.Com. We follow his Palanpur account and mention the other version.
He said about three years in his 2023 speech (PTI, ANI). PTI's 2024 Jai Hind report says nearly two years. We give both.

ANI's report, carried by NDTV and others, prints 'I have no agitations in saying'. The speech text published by Revoi reads 'I have no hesitation in saying', which is clearly what he said, so we quote that. Adani's wording elsewhere differs slightly by outlet; each quote follows the cited report.
His official profile says twelve; the group's site menu lists ten; Reuters said nine in 2025. We give no number.

disputed.note: The page displays media@adani.com, but the link behind it opens mediainfo@adaniports.com. We could not tell which is live, so neither is listed. We list the media contact printed on the group's October 2026 press release instead.
